lines.trans: Being summoned is a first for me, and you are the expert in that field.

words.gloss: since it is the first time

lines.trans: Dress neatly—wear a neat business suit.
To show deeper self-reflection, how about wearing traditional Korean attire?
Do that and they will mark you down as being defiant.
It seems you have to go to the Broadcast Standards Commission because of me—I feel awful.
Still, was that outfit not pretty that day? Back then you told me it looked pretty.
Anyway, as I said that day too, an outfit like that is trouble on public television.
Wait—was I getting scolded by you back then?
I am really not the sort of person to dwell on things in the past.
In that spirit, let's clink glasses and forget it all!
I do not drink beer.

meanings.note: Plain first-person singular pronoun used with friends, younger people, or subordinates; contracts to 난 with -는 and becomes 내가 before -가.

examples.trans: I'm going to stay home today.
I'll go first.

examples.text: 나는 출두가 또 처음이라, 네가 그쪽 분야에선 전문가잖아.
examples.trans: Being summoned is a first for me, and you are the expert in that field.
Here the word for 'appearing before a board' is key.
See you again!
It is raining again.
Let's start over from the beginning.
This is my first time coming to Seoul.
Do you have time today?
Where are you going?

meanings.note: Used only with close friends, younger people, or children
polite or indirect reference to the listener's group

examples.text: 그쪽에서 사전 녹화 좀 떠주면 안 되냐?
examples.trans: Couldn't your side pre-record them for us?
How are things on your side?

examples.text: 나는 출두가 또 처음이라, 네가 그쪽 분야에선 전문가잖아.
examples.trans: Being summoned is a first for me, and you are the expert in that field.
Here the word for 'in that field' is key.

examples.text: 나는 출두가 또 처음이라, 네가 그쪽 분야에선 전문가잖아.
examples.trans: Being summoned is a first for me, and you are the expert in that field.
Here the word for 'are an expert, you know' is key.
Dress neatly—wear a neat business suit.
This expression comes from 'neatly'.

meanings.note: Used for clothing worn on the body (shirts, pants, dresses, outfits).

examples.trans: I wore a black coat today.
It's cold, so please dress warmly.
Dress neatly—wear a neat business suit.
Here the word for 'formal suit' is key.
Please give me some water.
Please wait just a moment.
Please give me a little more.
It's further away.

examples.text: 좀 더 자숙하는 의미로 한복 입고 가면 어떨까?
examples.trans: To show deeper self-reflection, how about wearing traditional Korean attire?
This expression comes from 'reflecting contritely'.

examples.text: 좀 더 자숙하는 의미로 한복 입고 가면 어떨까?
examples.trans: To show deeper self-reflection, how about wearing traditional Korean attire?
Here the word for 'as a gesture of' is key.

examples.text: 좀 더 자숙하는 의미로 한복 입고 가면 어떨까?
examples.trans: To show deeper self-reflection, how about wearing traditional Korean attire?
Here the word for 'hanbok (traditional attire)' is key.

meanings.note: Basic verb of motion. With the respectful ending -세요 in 안녕히 가세요, it forms the polite farewell 'Goodbye!'. RR: gada.

examples.trans: I am going home.
Go safely!

meanings.en: to be how, to be in what state
meanings.note: Its adverbial form 어떻게 ('how') is used to ask how something is done or how things turned out.

examples.trans: How do you feel today?
How did the meeting turn out?

그러다.gloss: to say so; to do so

meanings.en: to say so; to speak like that
meanings.note: contracted from 그러하다; often follows quoted speech

meanings.en: to do so; to act like that

examples.trans: Who said that?
That friend also said they are going together.
Do that and they will mark you down as being defiant.
This expression comes from 'saying you are rebelling'.

meanings.note: Placed before the verb it modifies.

examples.trans: I finished all my homework.
I ate all the rice.

meanings.en: to get nicked, dented, or chipped

examples.trans: The car got a tiny nick.
The photo came out well.

meanings.note: Humble first-person singular pronoun used in polite speech.

examples.trans: I have an induction ceremony.
Follow me.

meanings.note: Usually followed by -e to mean 'because of'.

examples.trans: I was late because of the rain.
It's because of you.
I have to attend the Broadcast Commission meeting today.
The Broadcast Commission announced new regulations.

meanings.note: Takes a complement marked with 이/가.

examples.trans: I want to become a doctor.
It has already become 12 o'clock.

보다.gloss: to see, to watch; to take (an exam)

meanings.en: to see, to look at, to watch

examples.trans: I watched a movie on the weekend.
I took the driver's license exam.

meanings.note: Respectful, polite adjective used to apologize in workplaces and to strangers. Formal 죄송합니다 is the standard workplace apology. RR: joesonghada.

examples.trans: I am very sorry for being late.
I am sorry for the inconvenience.

meanings.en: what to do, how to act

examples.trans: What should we do?
What should we do? (2)

meanings.note: Colloquial contraction of 그런데; introduces a contrast or obstacle.
Used to shift the topic in conversation.

examples.trans: By the way, what time is it now?
I want to go. But I don't have time.

meanings.note: refers to a previously mentioned or specific day

examples.trans: We have lots of stages that day.
I don't have time that day.

meanings.note: refers to something known to both speakers or near the listener

examples.trans: That movie was really fun.
What is that person's name?
The outfit you're wearing today is really pretty.
It's cold, so please wear warm clothes.
The flowers are really pretty.
pretty clothes

않다.gloss: to not do, to not be

meanings.en: to not do, to not be
meanings.note: Auxiliary negative verb/adjective used after -지 (long-form negation)

examples.trans: The weather isn't cold today.
I didn't say anything.
Did you hear about this back then?
I was busy today because of back then.

meanings.en: to do, to perform, to hold
meanings.note: Core verb; also combines with nouns to form verbs.

examples.trans: What are you doing right now?
We are holding a meeting today.

examples.text: 암튼 내가 그날도 말했지만 공영방송에선 곤란해, 그런 옷.
examples.trans: Anyway, as I said that day too, an outfit like that is trouble on public television.
Here the word for 'anyway' is key.

meanings.note: Common verb for expressing thoughts in words.

examples.trans: Please speak slowly.
Speak loudly.
KBS is Korea's representative public broadcaster.
A new drama is starting on public broadcasting.

examples.text: 암튼 내가 그날도 말했지만 공영방송에선 곤란해, 그런 옷.
examples.trans: Anyway, as I said that day too, an outfit like that is trouble on public television.
This expression comes from 'is problematic'.

examples.text: 그런 실수는 누구나 할 수 있어요.
examples.trans: Anyone can make a mistake like that.
This is the first time I'm hearing a story like that.
Wait—was I getting scolded by you back then?
This expression comes from 'got scolded'.

meanings.note: Bound noun often contracted to 거 in everyday speech.

examples.trans: This is my bag.
Because I think I'm late.

meanings.note: Hangul spelling of the English abbreviation PD, widely used in Korean broadcasting.

examples.trans: Who is the PD in charge of the new program?

examples.text: 그녀는 예능 피디가 되기 위해 시험을 준비했다.
examples.trans: She prepared for the exam to become a variety PD.
Please don't say it like that.
It's not that difficult compared to what I thought.

meanings.en: to pass (of time) or go past (a place)
meanings.note: Its adnominal form 지난 ('past / last') is commonly used before time nouns, e.g., 지난 시즌.

examples.trans: Time passes really fast.
I watched a movie last weekend.

meanings.note: Sino-Korean numeral used with counters and in numbers

examples.trans: Let's meet in the first-floor lobby.

examples.text: 일 호선이 가장 오래된 지하철 노선이에요.
examples.trans: Line 1 is the oldest subway line.
About this.
Treat people.

examples.text: 내가 또 그렇게 지난 일에 대해서 연연하고 그런 사람은 아니에요.
examples.trans: I am really not the sort of person to dwell on things in the past.
This expression comes from 'dwelling on and'.

meanings.note: Can refer to a single person or people/a crowd in general without a plural suffix.

examples.trans: There are many people in the cafeteria.
He is a good person.

meanings.note: Negative copula used with nouns (often with -이/가)

examples.trans: It is not my fault.
Today is not Sunday, it's Monday.

meanings.note: 1st person plural pronoun; also used for 'my' with family, school, or workplace

examples.trans: Our team has a good atmosphere.
Let's eat lunch together tomorrow.

examples.text: 우리 그런 의미에서 짠하고 다 잊자!
examples.trans: In that spirit, let's clink glasses and forget it all!
This expression comes from 'clinking glasses and'.

examples.text: 피디가 마지막 순간까지 잊지 않아야 되는 게 뭔지 알아?
examples.trans: Do you know what a producer must never forget until the very last moment?

examples.text: 잊지 않고 꼭 갚아 줄 수 있어야 피디한테 힘이 생겨.
examples.trans: Only when people know you remember and repay every debt does a producer gain power.
I do not drink beer.
Here the word for 'as for beer' is key.

meanings.note: Short-form negation placed directly before verbs and adjectives

examples.trans: I'm not going to the office today.
I haven't watched that movie yet.
I want to drink right now.
How about trying to drink together tomorrow?

meanings.note: Used in standard farewells 안녕히 계세요 and 안녕히 가세요.

examples.trans: Goodbye! (to someone staying)
Goodbye! (to someone leaving)

meanings.note: Honorific equivalent of 있다; used in 안녕히 계세요 ('goodbye' to someone staying).

examples.trans: Goodbye! (to someone staying)
Is the teacher inside right now?
